title: I backtested 11 strategies with 8 years of data: none beat buy and hold
author: Strong_Appearance522

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: that's the honest result most people never post. over 8 years with 2020 and 2022 in it I'd check drawdown too, a couple might lose on return and still win on the worst year. grading rules against buy and hold on the same bars is what Quantradin does, I built it and it's free to use. quantradin.com  which one came closest?

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: thanks! drawdown is in the readme tables. closest was 12-month momentum checked monthly on QQQ over 20 years: 15.1%/yr vs 16.1% buy & hold, but worst drop was -29% vs -53%. so you’re right, a couple of them lost on return but held up much better in 2008/2020/2022. the 200-day trend filter on SPY was similar (-27% vs -55%).

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: -29% against -53% is the number I'd lead the readme with, more than the return. people sit through a slow year fine, almost nobody holds through a halving. did the momentum one spend most of 2022 in cash?

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: for 2022, it was only partly in cash. the 12m return was still positive through march so it held jan to april and ate about -21% (QQQ itself did about -32% for the year). it flipped to cash at the start of may 2022 and stayed out for 12 months, getting back in may 2023 at roughly the price it sold at. so it didn’t dodge the first leg, just the second half. funny thing is the -29% worst drop was actually covid, it held through march 2020 because the 12m return never turned negative

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: eating the first leg and sitting out the rest is about the best a 12 month lookback can do. the cost shows up on re-entry: buying back near the price it sold at means that year out in cash was roughly a wash against just holding.

comments.author: Infamous_Food_3766
comments.body: read the readme. does the cash balance earn any interest in the test? the aapl crossover table says it's invested 65% of the time, so i'd be curious to see that assumption next to the comparison. wouldn't assume it closes the gap, just useful to know what's included.

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: good catch, no, cash earns 0% in the test, and i should state that in the readme. rough estimate: aapl 20/50 was in cash \~35% of the time, so at typical t-bill rates over that decade it’d add maybe 0.5–1%/yr. doesn’t close a 15.6% vs 29.2% gap, but it matters more for the slow trend strategies that sit in cash for long stretches. might add a cash yield option.

replies.author: Infamous_Food_3766
replies.body: cheers for adding it. even if it does not close the gap, having that cash assumption written down makes the comparison much clearer.

comments.author: TheFertileSloth
comments.body: This is pretty on par with most backtesting I’ve done. You can definitely get an edge over just throwing a dart randomly, but it mostly prevents losses over increases gains. I found the better focus was trends by sector and the market regime.

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: yeah that matches what i saw. the trend/momentum rules mostly cut the crashes rather than adding return. sector + regime is a good shout. what did you use to define the regime, something like the index vs its 200-day, or volatility based?

replies.author: TheFertileSloth
replies.body: Fun question, both. Differentiating the general trends and being able to flag when things become quickly volatile is huge, but they should both consider one another if that makes sense. I tend to follow the volatility based as it can tell me “maybe not right now…” and sometimes cash is king.

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: makes sense, trend tells you where you are and vol tells you how fast it can go wrong. my rules are all trend/momentum so they only react after the drop has started, a vol filter could get out earlier. might try something like “go to cash when 20-day realized vol is above its 1-year average” on top of the 200-day rule and see if it cuts the drawdown more than it costs in return. cash is king is underrated lol

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: That's a common result, and an honest one, since beating buy and hold after costs is hard for simple rules. Before dropping them, I'd look at what each strategy did on risk, such as the worst drawdown and the time spent in the market, because a rule that makes less but falls much less can still be worth using. With 11 strategies tried, one of them beating the index by luck is also likely, so a negative result across all of them is reassuring in its own way. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to run a rule against history with fees and out-of-sample data.

replies.author: Strong_Appearance522
replies.body: agreed on all of it. drawdown and time in market are in the comparison tables, and that’s where the slow ones looked decent: spy 200-day trend cut the worst drop from -55% to -27% while keeping most of the return. and yeah, multiple testing showed up for real. one combo (30-min range breakout on tsla) looked great until i checked it year by year. nearly all the profit came from 2019-2021, and it went negative at slightly higher costs.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good that you checked it year by year, since a result that comes mostly from a few years and flips with slightly higher costs is a clear warning. The 200-day trend result is a useful one, with the worst drop cut roughly in half. I'd keep that one in the comparison and treat the TSLA breakout as a lesson in how fragile a good-looking test can be.

comments.author: CalmlyPrestigious

So you're not telling most people in the know anything new.
